ABSTRACT
Mixed pixels in hyperspectral images are a common imagination in the process of hyperspectral image pro-
cessing, usually processed using mixed pixel decomposition. To explore the effect of multi-source data fusion on
endmember bundle extraction, a multi-modal and multi-objective optimization endmember bundle extraction
method based on data fusion (MMO-CDPSO-RSADRDSM) is proposed. Firstly, the initialization particles are
randomly assigned in the region by DSM interference; Secondly, according to the characteristics of hyperspectral
image space and DSM space, the crowding distance of decision space is improved to improve the diversity of
decision space; Finally, the DSM derived weights are integrated into the optimization model to calculate the
objective function, and the endmember bundle is extracted iteratively by the above method. The effective
endmember bundles extracted by the MMO-CDPSO-RSADRDSM algorithm have mean RMSE (mRMSE) of 0.1853
and 0.1548 on MUUFL and Houston data, respectively, and recombinant minimum mSAD (re-min mSAD) of
0.0325 and 0.0341. The number of endmemebers extracted on the MUUFL dataset is 35, and in Houston it is 36.
The experimental results show that this method has good recognition ability for endmembers with high differ-
ences and similar hyperspectral bands, and extracts more effective endmember bundles on this basis. This
provides a new method for extracting endmember bundles for multi-source data fusion.
1. Introduction
Hyperspectral images have the advantages of hyperspectral resolu-
tion and spectral integration, and a complete high-resolution spectral
curve can be extracted according to each pixel ( Goetz et al.,1985 ). It has
been widely used in agricultural remote sensing ( Huang et al., 2023;
Kuswidiyanto et al., 2023; Dutta et al., 2024 ), forest monitoring ( Filippi
et al., 2022 ), rangeland ( Vermeulen et al., 2021 ), marine monitoring
( Hommersom et al., 2011; Gu et al., 2024 ), and other fields. However,
the performance of hyperspectral data such as signal-to-noise ratio and
spatial resolution is restricted to a certain extent, resulting in mixed
pixels. This affects image denoising and repair, feature extraction and
classification ( Li et al., 2023(a) ), object detection ( Yang et al., 2021; Yin
et al., 2023 ), and so on to a certain extent. Through spectral mixing
analysis, the observed spectral reflectance of a single pixel mixed by a
group of fixed-endmembers in the instantaneous field angle can be
decomposed, which is called mixed pixel decomposition. The spectral
characteristics of each type of ground object that can be extracted from it
are called endmembers, which determine the accuracy of the unmixing
( Keshava and Mustard, 2002 ).
According to whether there are pure pixels in the spectral data,
endmember extraction can be divided into endmember identification
algorithm (EIA) and endmember generation algorithm (EGA). EIA
directly extracts endmember from image data, while EGA assumes that
there is no pure pixel in the image, and generates endmember curve
through algorithm and image analysis. For most remote sensing images,
the problem of unmixing can be realized by the EIA. The method of
endmember extraction based on convex geometry theory was first pro-
posed, and the pure pixel index (PPI) method uses the characteristics of
the endmembers and vector projection properties of a single shape
formed by remote sensing images in the feature space for endmember
extraction ( Boardman,1993; Boardman et al., 1995 ). The N-FINDER
( Winter,1999; Luo et al.,2012 ) method is based on the linear spectral
mixture model, using the special structure of convex simplex in the
feature space of hyperspectral data, and obtaining all endmembers in the
image by finding the largest simplex. Its related variants have also been
proposed ( Wang et al.,2013; Chang and Chang, 2016 ). The vertex
component analysis (VCA) algorithm is based on the principle of

( Nascimento and Dias, 2005 ). For some specific application scenarios,
Triple-SMLM is used for shadow removal research on near ground
hyperspectral vegetation canopy, which solves the problems of shadow
overcompensation and false compensation ( Zhang et al., 2024 ). In
agricultural scenarios, the integration of sparse unmixing and segmen-
tation techniques enables the identification of bare land, harvested
fields, and high vegetation covered fields ( Sahadevan, 2021 ). The
biggest advantage of the above method is that the algorithm is simple
and time saving, but it is difficult to extract the complete endmember
combination from complex spectral images. At the same time, it is
impossible to solve the endmember combination whose data do not meet
the requirements of the simplex structure.
Data fusion has been proven to provide more useful information
( Chen et al., 2022 ). Fusing spatial and spectral information can fully
consider the relationship between pixels and objects ( Rogge et al.,
2007 ). Kowkabi ( Kowkabi et al.,2015; Kowkabi et al.,2017 ) proved
through experiments that using spatial information for preprocessing
can improve the effect of endmember extraction. The intelligent opti-
mization algorithm can transform the endmember extraction problem
into an optimization problem, which was first proposed by Zhang
( Zhang et al., 2011(a) ). DPSO algorithm realizes the optimal pure pixel
extraction by 0 and 1 encoding of particles combined with the improved
speed and position update method. Subsequently, numerous variants
emerged, which have a certain optimization effect on improving the
accuracy and efficiency of endmember extraction ( Liu et al., 2017(a) ).
Not only can the particle swarm optimization algorithm extract end-
members, but also the ant colony algorithm ( Zhang et al., 2011(b); Gao
et al., 2014 ), genetic algorithm ( Cheng et al., 2019 ), and differential
evolution algorithm ( Zhong et al., 2013 ) extract the optimal combina-
tion of endmembers.
The phenomenon of the same object with a different spectrum or the
same spectrum foreign matter on the remote sensing image will cause
the endmember of the same mixed pixel to have a different spectrum in
the image, resulting in spectral variability. By the endmember bundle
extraction (EBE), the effective endmembers reflecting the feature in-
formation are obtained. EBE was first proposed by Bateson, and the
highly correlated endmembers were manually selected to form the
endmember bundle ( Bateson et al., 2000 ). Subsequently, some algo-
rithms for the automatic extraction of endmember bundles have been
proposed. Among them, the clustering method has received extensive
attention. Somers ( Somers et al., 2012 ) and others randomly sampled
hyperspectral data to generate subsets. After analyzing all subsets, the
pure pixels of each subset were extracted by the endmember, and then K-
mean clustering was used. Euclidean distance was used as a similarity
measure, and the obtained endmember bundle was used as the input of
the MESMA algorithm to solve the abundance. Inspired by this model,
SSEBE( Xu et al.,2018 ) and SCEBE( Xu et al., 2015 ) have been proposed
successively. Ye( Ye et al., 2021 ) used VCA to extract the endmember of
sub-image blocks and used PCA to participate in the boundary extraction
and fusion in the screening of mixed pixels, then the SAD was used to
identify the candidate endmember to obtain an effective endmember
bundle. All the above methods obtain endmember bundles through
blocking, clustering, screening, and other operations. Its advantage is
that it can obtain more endmember bundles, but the blocking operation
ignores the relationship between sub-image blocks. At the same time, if
more sub-image blocks are divided, it is easy to obtain more endmem-
bers in the data, but it is not an effective endmember bundle composed
of endmembers. The intelligent optimization algorithm is less explored
in endmember bundle extraction. Liu proposed two algorithms, IQPSO
and MODPSO. IQPSO ( Du et al., 2019 ) method does not need to predict
the number of the endmember bundle and determines whether the
extracted endmember is an invalid solution through extreme recon-
struction error. Although the effect of automatic extraction of
endmember bundles by this method is better than that based on clus-
tering, the algorithm uses an iterative mechanism and sets a threshold to
control the cumulative number of times the algorithm runs, so the ef-
ficiency of the algorithm is low. MODPSO ( Liu et al., 2017(b) ) algorithm
takes endmember extraction as a multi-objective optimization analysis
and uses DPSO ’ s 0 and 1 particle encoding method and speed and po-
sition update method. Although the efficiency is higher than IQPSO, the

This research work is structured as follows: Section 2 introduces the
research methods and materials. The test results and discussion are
described in section 3 . Finally, Section 4 is the conclusion and prospect

2. Methods and materials
Spectral unmixing depends on the scene mixture model, and large-
scale spectral mixing can be considered as a linear mixing problem.
This paper mainly focuses on the linear mixture model to explore the
problem of mixed pixels. Meanwhile, to enable the algorithm to effec-
tively understand the fused data and extract effective endmember
bundles, a fusion of DSM and hyperspectral imaging proposes an end-
member bundle extraction method based on multi-modal and multi-
objective optimization. This algorithm fully considers the interaction
between multi-source data in particle initialization, particle updates,
and particle sorting, enabling more effective bundle outputs.

ABSTRACT
In this study, we explore spectral heterogeneity within plant canopies, a characteristic often observed in stressed
plants where certain leaves or intra-leaf regions exhibit stress symptoms while others remain unaffected.
Considering this variability in spectral signatures holds promise for enhancing remote sensing methodologies
aimed at plant stress detection. Typically, remote sensing techniques analyze the plant as a whole, potentially
overlooking stress-related spectral signatures due to the inclusion of unaffected pixels. We used a clustering-
based technique, which incorporates semi-supervised learning elements for tuning hyper-parameters, to differ -
entiate spectral patterns associated with and unique to pixels from broomrape-infected ( Orobanche spp. and
Phelipanche spp.) carrots from unrelated patterns. Ground-based hyperspectral (400 – 1000 nm) images of
broomrape-infected and non-infected carrot canopies were used in an agglomerative clustering procedure fol -
lowed by spectral angle mapper (SAM) analysis to identify a spectral endmember indicative of broomrape
infection symptoms. Pixels from this cluster constituted an average of 8.5 – 11.5 % from the canopies of infected
plants. Subsequently, we: (a) examined the relationship between carrot leaf mineral content and the percentage
of symptomatic pixels to explore stress-induced alterations creating the unique spectral signatures of infected
plants; and (b) utilized the inverse mode of PROSPECT, a radiative transfer model (RTM), to derive primary plant
traits from the distinct spectral data of each cluster. We found that deficits in two macro elements, phosphorous
and potassium, along with two pigments, chlorophyll and carotenoid, were correlated with the symptomatic
cluster in infected plants. The methodology presented in this study paves the way for further research into
broomrape detection in various crop species, as well as other plant stressors.
1. Introduction
Broomrapes ( Orobanche spp. and Phelipanche spp.) are root parasitic
weeds significantly hindering the cultivation of numerous vegetable and
field crops worldwide. These chlorophyll-lacking holoparasitic plants
attach to the host plant by forming haustoria (vascular connections)
with the host ’ s roots. Then, the parasite becomes a sink and depletes
water, nutrients, and minerals from the host for its own development,
including tubercle production, apex formation, and the emergence of
inflorescences above the soil surface ( Parker, 2012 ). Carrot ( Daucus
carota, Apiaceae ) is a high-income cash crop widely grown throughout
Europe and the Mediterranean area. Two species of broomrape, Oro -
banche crenata and Phelipanche aegyptiaca parasitize the carrot roots and
in highly infested fields, can cause total yield loss ( Bernhard et al., 1998;
Cochavi et al., 2016b; Parker, 2012 ).
Herbicide application is the most effective method to control
broomrape in carrots and other crop species. The primary limitation of
existing chemical control protocols is the uniform application of

festations within the fields ( Cohen et al., 2017; Eizenberg and Gold -
wasser, 2018 ). Adopting site-specific weed management (SSWM)
approaches becomes imperative. Nonetheless, as most of the parasite ’ s
life cycle occurs below the soil surface, detecting parasitized plants in
the field through remote sensing presents a formidable challenge.
Recently, several studies investigated the potential to detect
broomrape-infected plants by remote sensing of the host plants. These
preliminary studies, conducted on sunflowers, demonstrated that plants
parasitized with sunflower broomrape ( Orobanche cumana ) exhibited
differences in spectral reflectance ( Atsmon et al., 2022; Cochavi et al.,
2017; Ortiz-Bustos et al., 2016 ) and morphological attributes ( Lati et al.,
2019 ) compared to non-infected plants. Atsmon et al., (2022) also
demonstrated the feasibility to utilize these differences for classification
between infected and non-infected plants. An alternative approach for
broomrape detection involves employing physically-based models ac -
counting for the mechanistic link between measured data and plant
traits. Until now, models demonstrated for broomrape detection have
been empirical, relying on ML algorithms or statistical models focusing
exclusively on improving classification accuracy. Empirical methods
often overlook variables influencing remote sensing data accuracy,
including image acquisition conditions, sun-view angle geometry, and
the crop ’ s architecture and phenological stage ( Jafarbiglu and Pourreza,
2023 ), rendering the transferability of such classification models un -
certain ( Wang et al., 2023 ). In contrast, physically-based approaches,
leveraging the inversion of radiative transfer models (RTMs), have been
suggested to achieve robust remote sensing of crops ( F ´eret et al., 2019;
Li et al., 2018; Shiklomanov et al., 2016 ). PROSPECT, for instance, is an
optical model capable of simulating reflectance and transmittance at the
leaf level across the electromagnetic spectrum from 400 nm to 2500 nm
( F ´eret et al., 2021 ). When operated in the inverse mode, PROSPECT can
retrieve primary plant traits from spectral data. Combining RTMs and
ML algorithms, simulated data generated by the RTM can be used to
train a statistical model, which is eventually applied to real spectral
observations ( Peanusaha et al., 2024 ).
An important insight gained by previous broomrape detection
studies revealed a non-uniform spectral response within canopies of
infected plants. Ortiz-Bustos et al., (2016) showed significant differences
in the levels of red and far-red fluorescence reflected by infected and
non-infected plants depended on the leaf pairs (e.g., 1st and 2nd vs. 3rd
and 4th). Similar trend was observed by Atsmon et al., (2022) that
showed the impact of the spatial location of the sampled area within the
crop canopy (leaf center vs. edges) on the classification accuracy be -
tween infected and non-infected plants. Considering this variation
within the canopy response to the broomrape-related stress has potential
to benefit future research and practice of remote sensing of broomrape
infected plants. These attempts to address spectral heterogeneity within
broomrape-infected canopies required manual labeling of suspected
symptomatic regions within the plant ( Atsmon et al., 2022; Ortiz-Bustos
et al., 2016 ). However, recent advancements in sensors, computing ca -
pabilities, and image processing systems have ushered in new data
analysis methodologies enhancing the automation, precision, and
robustness in identifying symptomatic regions in stressed plants ( Jin
et al., 2021; Singh et al., 2016 ). In a recent study, Omidi et al. (2022)
suggested a semi-supervised approach to cluster symptomatic and
asymptomatic leaves in root lesion nematode-infected walnut trees. An
agglomerative style of hierarchical clustering based on leaf-level
hyperspectral measurements was applied to identify a symptomatic
cluster unique to infected plants. This technique could cluster asymp -
tomatic leaves of infected trees with healthy leaves from non-infected
trees, based on their spectral similarity, thereby isolating the symp -
tomatic leaves to better represent the stress ’ spectral signature. The
development of such methodologies for identification of stress symp -
tomatic regions at the intra-plant level holds substantial promise for
various aspects related to remote sensing of plant stress, including
broomrape-infected plants.

employed. Symptomatic and asymptomatic pixels were clustered from
hyperspectral images of broomrape-infected and non-infected carrot
plants at early, pre-symptomatic stages. Subsequently, a new method -
ology was developed, leveraging the clustering capability for broomrape
symptomatic pixels to improve

2.3. Ground truth measurements of broomrape infection levels
Broomrapes that had already flowered are likely to have a more
significant cumulated effect on the host than tubercles that are yet to
flower. Therefore, the final values of infection levels ( Fig. 2 ) were
calculated by multiplying the number of tubercles at tubercle stages of
S4 ( Eizenberg et al., 2004 ) by three and adding the number of tubercles
at tubercle stages of S1-S3, as follows:
A = 3B + C
Where A is the calculated infection level, B is the number of
broomrape inflorescences, and C is the number of broomrape tubercles.
2.4. Hyperspectral data
Plants were imaged using a ground-based hyperspectral camera
(Specim IQ, Specim Ltd., Oulu, Finland) that relies on a push-broom line
scanner mounted on an internal rotating stage. The camera provides
images of 512 × 512 pixels with 204 spectral bands between 400 and
1000 nm. The spectral resolution is 7 nm at full width half maximum
(FWHM). Each image included five plants, in a random order, allowing a
short image acquisition timeframe (11:00 A.M – 12:00 P.M), thereby
reducing environmental variables during data collection. In addition, a
white reference panel was placed in each frame to calibrate the raw data
and account for changes in lighting conditions. The camera ’ s built-in
calibration procedure produced calibrated reflectance values during
the image acquisition steps ( Behmann et al., 2018 ). The camera was
mounted on a tripod, and the distance between the camera lens and the
top end of the plant canopy was 0.5 – 1 m ( Fig. 1 a). In this range, the
spatial resolution of one pixel is about 1 mm. Imaging was performed
outside with the sun as the light source for illumination, and the scan -
ning integration time was set to a minimum of 1 ms per line. 147
hyperspectral images were taken of the whole canopy of the carrot plant.
Normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) and excess green index
(EGI) were used to mask out background pixels ( Fig. 1 d).
2.5. Sample clustering and SAM analysis
In our approach, we utilized the agglomerative style of hierarchical
clustering as suggested by Omidi et al., (2022) for this type of dataset
and objectives. This method of clustering is superior in handling com -
plex and high-dimensional hyperspectral data, supports any pairwise
distance metric and performs well on common clustering test cases ( El-
Hamdouchi and Willet, 1989 ). While the core algorithm, agglomerative
hierarchical clustering, operates unsupervised, semi-supervised learning
elements were incorporated in the hyper-parameter optimization phase.
This was facilitated primarily through fine-tuning the distance
threshold, which was informed by prior knowledge about the charac -
teristic cluster of infected samples.
Complete linkage, which uses the maximum distances between all
observations of two sets, was chosen to prevent intermediate samples
between dense clusters from fusing those dissimilar dense clusters.
Testing with other linkage methods, such as single linkage, produced
poor clustering relative to complete linkage and were not used further.
Cosine, which measures the angular similarity between two vectors, was
set as the affinity type. Cosine was chosen as it performs well and
commonly used with high-dimensional data, such as hyperspectral
matrices.
Employing agglomerative clustering on all pixels from 147 hyper -
spectral images suffers from intrinsic computational complexity as the
algorithm relies on a distance metric that grows quadraticaly in size as
the number of samples increases. Therefore, a two-step process was
developed for making the analyses feasible. Clustering was initially
performed per each plant individually, resulting with a significant
decrease in representative spectra. A fixed distance threshold of 0.002 %
was used as it was found to reduce the number of samples in each image
to between 20 and 250, thus still preserving the spectral heterogeneity of
the image ( Fig. 3 a and Fig. 3 b). In the second step, agglomerative
clustering was performed on all retrieved spectra from the first step (n =

control and infected treatments facilitated to enhance the specificity of
the model to the unique aspects of our research. A candidate cluster for
representing broomrape stress contains symptomatic pixels which come
exclusively from infected plants and not from control plants. Ideally, the
candidate cluster would include samples from several different infected
plants, i.e., a spectral pattern common among different broomrape
infected plants. The distance threshold for clustering was tuned to

Cross-Scale Validation of Hyperspectral Unmixing
Over Agricultural Landscapes
Haris Ampas

Abstract—In heterogeneous agricultural landscapes, hyper-
spectral pixels often contain mixtures of soil and vegetation,
making reliable subpixel characterization essential. This letter
introduces a multisensor validation methodology for soil and
vegetation-fraction estimates using Planet’s Tanager-1 hyper-
spectral imagery (30 m), very-high-resolution (VHR) uncrewed
aerial vehicle (UA V) imagery, and ﬁeld-measured endmember
spectra. Validation combines: 1) distribution-level agreement with
UA V-derived vegetation cover; 2) spectral consistency with ﬁeld
reference spectra; and 3) spatial coherence with landscape struc-
ture. We demonstrate our approach on a heterogeneous vineyard
scene using an autoencoder-based spectral unmixing (AE-SU) and
fully constrained least squares (FCLS) as a standard supervised
baseline. Results show that distribution-level metrics remain
informative under cross-scale resolution mismatch, with AE-SU
achieving closer agreement with the UA V-derived vegetation cover
than FCLS (Overlap 0.80 versus 0.72 and Jensen–Shannon (JS)
0.059 versus 0.079). High-abundance pixels are also spectrally
consistent with ﬁeld-measured endmembers, while the resulting
fraction maps preserve coherent spatial structure. These ﬁndings
support practical cross-scale validation of unmixing outputs in
mixed-pixel agricultural landscapes.
Index Terms—Autoencoder, fractional cover, multiscale valida-
tion, Planet Tanager-1, spectral unmixing, vegetation suppression.
I. I NTRODUCTION
H
YPERSPECTRAL imagery is widely used in agricul-
ture, where detailed spectral signatures support soil and
vegetation analysis at the ﬁeld scale, enabling soil-property
estimation [1], [2] and characterization of vegetation condition
and structure [3]. However, the coarse spatial resolution of
satellite hyperspectral sensors (>30 m) produces mixed pixels
in heterogeneous ﬁelds, where soil and vegetation coexist (e.g.,
vineyards or orchards). A major challenge is that vegetation
often obscures the soil signal within these mixed pixels,
limiting the accuracy of soil-property retrieval. This is par-
ticularly critical for applications such as soil organic carbon
(SOC) estimation, where even small vegetation fractions can

Recent work has highlighted the importance of estimating
subpixel soil and vegetation proportions. In our previous study
on bare-soil detection using EnMAP hyperspectral imagery
[6], spectral unmixing showed clear advantages over index-
based thresholding for identifying soil-dominant pixels. The
evaluation relied on fractional cover maps from Sentinel-2
composites, which are well suited for large-area assessment
but leave open questions at ﬁner spatial scales, especially in
heterogeneous ﬁelds.
Validating abundance estimates is challenging because accu-
rate reference fractions are rarely available under conditions
comparable to hyperspectral data. High-resolution uncrewed
aerial vehicle (UA V) imagery can provide detailed vegeta-
tion masks, but diﬀerences in spatial resolution, geolocation
accuracy, and sensor characteristics introduce uncertainties
that make direct spatial correspondence unreliable [7], [8].
As a result, many validation approaches rely on indirect
indicators (e.g., reconstruction error), which do not fully
capture how well unmixing performs on real, heterogeneous
scenes. Therefore, there is a need for a practical validation
procedure that can leverage high-resolution observations while
acknowledging the limitations of cross-scale comparison.
This work addresses that need by providing a methodology
to assess subpixel soil and vegetation estimates from satellite
imagery using very-high-resolution (VHR) UA V data and
ﬁeld-measured endmembers. The novelty of the proposed
methodology relies on leveraging these complementary per-
spectives to oﬀer a robust and interpretable basis for evaluat

The remainder of this letter is organized as follows.
Section II describes the satellite, UA V , and ﬁeld data.
Section III presents the unmixing models and validation cri-

II. D ATASET
A. Satellite and Field Hyperspectral Data
The hyperspectral satellite data used in this study were
acquired by the Tanager-1 sensor operated by Planet [9]
on July 12, 2025, covering the agricultural landscape of
the Gerovasiliou Vineyard in Epanomi, Thessaloniki, Greece
(latitude 40.449◦, longitude 22.924 ◦). Launched on August
26, 2024, Tanager-1 provides full visible–shortwave infrared
(VSWIR) coverage (400–2500 nm) with 424 contiguous spec-
tral bands and a 30-m ground sampling distance, oﬀering
suﬃcient spectral detail (5 nm spectral resolution) for subpixel
vegetation analysis (Fig. 1, left).
Field reference spectra were collected using a PSR+ 3500
spectroradiometer (Spectral Evolution Inc., Lawrence,
MA, USA), which covers the 350−2500-nm range using
a 512-element silicon photodiode array (350−1000 nm;
2.8-nm spectral resolution) and two 256-element InGaAs
arrays (970−1910 nm; 8-nm resolution and 1900−2500 nm;
6-nm resolution). All measurements were acquired using a
bare ﬁber under ambient illumination and calibrated with a
Spectralon reference panel. The campaign took place during
the same week as the satellite overpass (July 17, 2025), under
comparable temperature and humidity conditions, ensuring
temporal and environmental consistency. The measured spectra
were resampled to the Tanager wavelength grid and used to
initialize the spectral unmixing model and support the pure-
pixel spectral validation. Field spectra were collected at three
vineyard locations, with ﬁve measurements per endmember
(soil and vegetation) at each location. Measurements were
acquired at 0.5 m under natural illumination and averaged
per class to derive representative endmembers. As the scene
is dominated by grapevines, vegetation is represented by a
single canopy endmember.
B. UA V V egetation Mask
A high-resolution vegetation mask (3 cm) was generated
using data acquired from a UA V ﬂight on July 17, 2025,
(Fig. 1, center) conducted at an altitude of 90 m over the
vineyard. The ﬂight was performed using a DJI Mavic 3
equipped with an RGB camera, and the collected images
were stitched into an orthomosaic covering the entire study
area. From this mosaic, the Excess Green (ExG) index was
computed for all pixels (Fig. 1, right)

To select a robust threshold, an Otsu-derived value (30) was
perturbed within a±5 interval, yielding comparable vegetation

The UA V-derived binary vegetation mask was aggregated to
the 30 m Tanager resolution by computing, for each Tanager
pixel, the proportion of UA V pixels classiﬁed as vegetation,
yielding a fractional cover reference map. Because of the large
spatial resolution diﬀerence between the UA V and satellite
data, pixel-level alignment is sensitive to geolocation oﬀsets.
Therefore, validation is performed by comparing vegetation-
fraction distributions and their consistency with the scene
geometry.

D. Distribution-Based V alidation Metrics
Validation is performed at the distribution level by com-
paring normalized histograms of predicted and UA V-derived
vegetation fractions, as pixelwise comparison is unreliable [8].
We evaluate similarity with a comprehensive set of met-
rics [7], [8]: histogram-bin mean absolute error (MAE), L2
distance, Earth Mover’s distance (EMD), histogram overlap,
Bhattacharyya coeﬃcient, cosine similarity, Jensen–Shannon
(JS) divergence, Pearson correlation, and Kling–Gupta eﬃ-
ciency (KGE) (Table I). These metrics quantify comple-
mentary aspects of error magnitude, mass displacement,
distribution aﬃnity, information content, and statistical cor-
respondence.
E. Pure-Pixel Spectral Consistency V alidation
To assess whether high predicted abundances correspond to
physically realistic material spectra, we examine the spectral
identity of the pixel with the highest abundance for each
endmember. For both soil and vegetation, we compare this
pixel’s spectrum against the corresponding ﬁeld-measured
endmember.

to spectrally plausible pixels, we compare each ﬁeld-measured

Abstract
Spectroscopy has become an extensively used tool for non-destructive high throughput
analysis of plant characteristics such as crop health, stress response, and photosynthetic prop-
erties. Hyperspectral cameras and compact spectrometers are common instruments used in
agriculture research and field applications to capture the vegetation reflectance spectrum at
the canopy scale (about one meter from top of the crop). Although hyperspectral imaging
(HSI) allows the isolation of the vegetation spectrum by pixel classification, collecting a clean
HSI dataset in the field is challenging due to motion artifacts and storage requirements for
extensive areas. A compact spectrometer system is a quicker and smaller data size alterna-
tive used for high throughput phenotyping applications. However, this instrument produces
a mixed reflectance signal at canopy scale as it integrates all the spectral signals of the scene
components within the field of view of the sensor.
This study explores the possibility of estimating an isolated vegetation reflectance from a
mixed signal using abundance estimates and color information of the scene components. An
HSI and a multi-instrument setup built with a compact spectrometer, RGB (red-green-blue)
and NIR (near infrared) cameras were used to sample data at canopy scale. The tradi-
tional spectral unmixing model and a variation that includes a color-matching process were
tested in this study as methods to obtain an isolated vegetation reflectance from a mixed
signal. Both spectral unmixing models were evaluated by observing the differences between
extracted and estimated endmembers reflectance in a recreated dataset derived from HSI
data that represents the multi-instrument setup. The model with color matching showed
less estimation error and less sensitivity to noisy inputs in the recreated dataset, and exhib-
ited similar response patterns between the multi-instrument and recreated datasets. This
indicates the potential of the proposed method as an alternative for estimating an isolated
vegetation spectrum from a mixed signal in applications at the canopy scale.

of specialty crops by hyperspectral imaging
Usman A. Zahidia, Krystian Łukasika, Grzegorz Cielniaka

UK, Riseholme Park, Lincoln, LN2 2BJ, United Kingdom
Abstract
The maturity classification of specialty crops such as strawberries and toma-
toes is an essential agricultural downstream activity for selective harvesting
and quality control (QC) at production and packaging sites. Recent advance-
ments in Deep Learning (DL) have produced encouraging results in color im-
ages for maturity classification applications. However, hyperspectral imaging
(HSI) outperforms methods based on color vision as it captures changes in
biological attributes, such as an abundance of pigment (anthocyanin and ly-
copene) and chlorophyll catabolism during the maturity process, by spectral
variation. Multivariate analysis methods and Convolutional Neural Networks
(CNN) deliver promising results; however, a large amount of input data and
the associated preprocessing requirements cause hindrances in practical ap-
plication. Conventionally, the reflectance intensity in a given electromagnetic
spectrum is employed in estimating fruit maturity. We present a feature ex-
traction method to empirically demonstrate that the peak reflectance in sub-
bands such as 500-670 nm (pigment band) and the wavelength of the peak
position, and contrarily, the trough reflectance and its corresponding wave-
length within 671–790 nm (chlorophyll band) are convenient to compute
yet distinctive features for the maturity classification. The proposed feature
selection method is beneficial because preprocessing, such as dimensionality
reduction, isavoidedbeforeeveryprediction, andtheamountofrequireddata
for model training is smaller when compared to State-Of-The-Art (SOTA)
methods, which eases its deployment. The feature set is designed to capture
these traits. The best SOTA methods, among 3D-CNN, 1D-CNN, and SVM,
achieve at most 90.0 % accuracy for strawberries and 92.0 % for tomatoes on
our dataset. Results show that the proposed method outperforms the SOTA
as it yields an accuracy above 98.0 % in strawberry and 96.0 % in tomato

classification. A comparative analysis of the time efficiency of these methods
is also conducted, which shows the proposed method performs prediction at
13 Frames Per Second (FPS) compared to the maximum 1.16 FPS attained
by the full-spectrum SVM classifier.
Keywords: Robotic harvesting, Strawberry, Tomato, Maturity estimation,
Hyperspectral imaging.
1. Introduction
Strawberry is a high-value and nutritious fruit with formidable economic
value. It is non-climacteric, which implies that it is not attributed to post-
harvest ripening. Moreover, its shelf life is also limited. Therefore, it is vital
to ascertain the right time for harvesting. Conversely, tomatoes are medium-
value and climacteric fruits with more significant production and consump-
tion scales. Moreover, the QC procedures at distributors and supermarkets
ensure that anomalous fruits do not end up in the end-user. Thus, maturity
stage estimation in both fruits is essential. Due to the sensitivity of the task,
expert human harvesters and QC personnel are employed worldwide. How-
ever, many key production areas (e.g., UK, US, NL, ES, JP) are now facing
severe labor shortages; therefore, developing alternative robotic harvesting
and packaging solutions is inevitable. Identifying the correct maturity stage
of strawberries and tomatoes is crucial. The maturity classification algo-
rithms have been the topic of interest in the research community for decades
[1] due to their application in selective harvesting [2] and quality control pro-
cedures [3]. Many deep learning and feature-based approaches address this
problem by employing color and hyperspectral vision.
1.1. Color Vision
Contemporary state-of-the-art DL is employed to estimate the maturity
stages of specialty crops with feature-based approaches using color images.
The application in strawberry maturity classification includes several re-
search contributions such as [4] applied YOLOv3 model for classifying eight
maturity levels with a mean Average Precision (mAP) of 0.89. [5] com-
pared feature-based and CNN classification and reported that CNNs better
classify unripe strawberries. However, they found that penalized multino-
mial regression has an accuracy of 86.4 %. Similarly, [6] compared several
feature-based approaches with CNN and reported the supremacy of CNNs

with 88.0 % accuracy.[7] used a dark channel enhancement algorithm to pre-
process strawberry images taken at night and finally achieved a ripeness

NetB2 as the best classifier with 73.0 % accuracy. Similarly, [9] applied
SE-YOLOv3-MobileNetV1 network to classify tomato maturity with higher
speed and mAP of 0.97. [2] employed Mask-RCNN-based instance segmen-
tation on strawberry with Resnet-50 backbone on 100 images that achieved
an average detection precision rate of 95.8 %, a recall rate of 95.4 %, and
a mean intersection over union (mIoU) rate of 89.8 %. Similarly, in the
domain of tomato classification, many DL models are applied, such as [10]
proposed a convolutional transformer for tomato maturity classification on
color images surpassing the state-of-the-art on common benchmark datasets.
[11] employed Yolov5m and Yolov5m combined with ResNet-50, ResNet-101,
and EfficientNet-B0, respectively, for classifying tomato fruit on the vine
into three classes: ripe, immature, and damaged with an accuracy of 97 %.
[12] developed a Faster R-CNN model named MatDet for tomato maturity
detection, which uses ResNet-50 as the backbone and RoIAlign to obtain
more precise bounding boxes and a Path Aggregation Network to address

[14] applied fuzzy classification architecture on the RGB color model with
descriptors to achieve the classification result withM SE of 0.537 × 10−3. A
few classical feature-based classification approaches are also employed, such

two stages of storage for their model in TomatoScan, which was also able to
determine the ripening stage of tomatoes with an overall accuracy of 75.0

Although deep learning models produce excellent results with accuracy

differing numbers. Therefore, a comparative analysis could not be drawn
directly.
Like computer vision, Deep learning is applied for crop maturity classi-

Abstract—Selecting a correct endmember subset from a large
number of endmembers plays an important role in improving
the performance of spectral unmixing. Sparse unmixing (SU)
provides a useful tool to solve this endmember selection problem.
However, due to the complexity of endmembers in the spectral
library and noise in hyperspectral data, this problem is ill-
posed and remains a signiﬁcant challenge. To address this, prior
information can be employed to mitigate the problem. Existing
algorithms, however, often overlook the possibility that the prior
information may be incomplete or inaccurate, and consider
only a single prior model. To this end, this article proposes an
adaptive method designed to handle incorrect prior information
and balance the tradeoﬀ between the contributions of two sets
of priors. In contrast to the conventional models, our method
dynamically adjusts optimal decision boundaries by introducing
decision-making parameters (DMPs), thereby obtaining a better
solution. Optimal weight conditions and robustness analysis
are also presented to prove the performance of our method.
Furthermore, experiments conducted on both simulated and
real datasets demonstrate that the proposed method delivers
robust and reliable performance, highlighting its eﬀectiveness in
addressing the unmixing challenges. The code of our method is
available at https://github.com/spdelphi/Double-Prior.
Index Terms—Adaptive prior model, double prior model,
endmember selection, hyperspectral remote sensing, sparse
regression, spectral unmixing.
I. I NTRODUCTION

PARSE unmixing (SU) is a semi-supervised unmixing
method that employs a known large endmember spectral
library to model mixed pixels. Based on the data charac-
teristics, SU identiﬁes an optimal subset of endmembers
from the library to best represent each mixed pixel [1].
The performance of SU largely depends on the coherence

of endmembers within mixed pixels [1], [2], [3]. Low coher-
ence and high sparsity generally favor the unmixing process.
However, the spectral library often exhibits high correlation
among endmembers. Moreover, using a large spectral library
will render the unmixing process more vulnerable to noise
interference [4]. As shown in [5, Th. 2], satisfying the
conditions for exact recovery of endmembers becomes increas-
ingly challenging under these circumstances. Consequently,
the unmixing problem is ill-posed, as numerous potential
endmember combinations can reconstruct the mixed pixels.
In this situation, selecting a correct endmember subset plays a
critical role in improving the performance of unmixing, which
is referred to as the endmember selection problem in this
article.
SU can be divided into the following seven categories, i.e.,
brute force algorithms, greedy algorithms, sparse Bayesian
algorithms, nonconvex optimization algorithms, multiobjec-
tive optimization algorithms, convex relaxation algorithms,
and deep learning (DL) algorithms [6], [7], [8], [9], [10].
Brute force algorithms operate by exhaustively enumerating
all possible combinations to determine the optimal solution.
While this approach ensures comprehensive exploration, it is
computationally intensive and may still yield multiple feasible
solutions [11], [12], [13]. Greedy algorithms are, however,
prone to suboptimal performance due to the high correla-
tion within the spectral library, often converging on a local
optimum. Sparse Bayesian algorithms utilize a statistical repre-
sentation for the endmembers to infer the posterior probability
density of the abu

To guarantee the endmember selection and unmixing per-
formance, the minimum coeﬃcient condition (MCC) and the
nonlinearity versus subset coherence condition (NSCC) must
be held [5], [36]. Unfortunately, these conditions are not
easy to satisfy due to the noise, spectral variability, and
high coherence of the spectral library [37]. Fig. 1(a) displays
one of the problems. The hyperplane of solution (solid line)
is parallel to the solid boundary (solid “diamond”) of the
model. It is impossible to have a sparse solution. For a
comprehensive overview of the geometric interpretation of
sparse models, please refer to [38]. To alleviate this dilemma,
some prior information about the scene can be useful. See Fig.
1(a), it is conceivable that the prior (the dashed boundary)
will result in the algorithm arriving at the correct solution.
Therefore, the prior provides critical insights into the presence
of speciﬁc materials within pixels [39], [40]. For this kind of
algorithm, the SU using spectral a priori information (SUnSPI)
incorporates the spectral a priori information into SU, thereby
demonstrating that this prior information is advantageous for
endmember selection and abundance estimation [41]. The
bandwise model based on spectral prior information (BMSPI)
further considers the inﬂuence of noise in diﬀerent spectral
bands, eﬀectively mitigating the eﬀects of spectral library
correlation and image noise on unmixing [42]. The knowl-
edge graph embedding spectral unmixing (KGESU) integrates
the geoscience knowledge graph into the unmixing process
in order to provide additional knowledge for endmember
selection [40].
However, it is hard to guarantee the accuracy of the prior
for each pixel. The unreliable priors may encounter many
problems. Fig. 1(b) and (c) displays two embarrassing sit-
uations. In Fig. 1(b), the prior weight (the solid boundary)
for the active endmember is too small, and the Lagrangian
parameter of the ℓ1 norm is not accurately detected. In this
case, it becomes the unconstrained ordinary least squares.
It should be noted that although the augmented Lagrangian
and alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMMs)
can estimate the Lagrangian parameter and converge to a
stable point, the choice of the parameter of the ℓ1 norm
is still a problem. Therefore, we indiscriminately summa-
rize these problems as Lagrangian parameter problems. As
illustrated in Fig. 1(c), the prior weight (the solid boundary)
for the inactive endmember is too small, leading to another
solution ˆx.
To handle these problems, two sets of candidate priors can
be considered for unmixing. In this way, even if one prior is
wrong, it can be corrected by another prior. This motivates us
to develop an adaptive algorithm to optimally leverage multi-
ple sets of priors, named adaptive SU (ADSU). Intuitively,
this method utilizes a variable “diamond” to identify the
sparse solution, whereas traditional methods merely expand
the “diamond,” preserving its shape, as shown in [27] and [38].
Consequently, this advantage can be leveraged to obtain a more
optimal solution. Refer to Fig. 1(b) again. As the boundary
undergoes a gradual transition from the dashed to the solid
one, the algorithm can obtain the correct solution when it ﬁrst
meets the hyperplane. Fig. 1(c) illustrates that another prior
(the dashed boundary) can prevent the wrong prior and obtain a
better solution x′. Fig. 1(d) illustrates another example. Due to
the slightly large Lagrangian parameter, neither model yields
the correct solution. However, we can still determine the best
one. More theoretical analyses are presented in this article.
The main contributions of this article can be enumerated as
follows.
1) We develop an adaptive model of double sets of priors
through the incorporation of decision-making parameters
(DMPs). The utilization of DMPs is expected to ensure
the optimal utilization of diﬀerent sets of priors, thereby
maximizing the eﬃcacy of the model.
2) We provide systematic analyses of the behavior

A B S T R A C T
Accurate detection of pests is vital in smart agriculture as it is among the main factors that profoundly
influence the yield and quality of crops. In the actual field, pests frequently manifest as small objects, thereby
presenting a considerable obstacle to effectively detect pests in the field. For the problem of ineffective
utilization of plant context information and inadequate design of neural architecture in field pest detection,
we propose the pest detection model (PestNAS) based on adaptive feature fusion and evolutionary neural
architecture search. It consists of the adaptive feature fusion module: plant context information is extracted,
and the adaptive fusion of pest-related features and plant auxiliary features is designed to effectively utilize
plant information; the evolutionary search space module: the novel search space that includes resolution and
receptive field enhancement operations is designed with evolution to improve pest representation; the GA-
Adam search algorithm: the Adam with genetic algorithm is designed to optimize the objective function of
neural architecture search and obtain the relatively better neural architecture for pest detection. The ablation
experiments verify the effectiveness of each module in the PestNAS. The comparison experiments reveal that
the PestNAS can achieve higher detection accuracy than the other ten neural architecture search models on
eleven field pests.
1. Introduction
The growth and yield of agricultural crops are influenced by many
elements ( Oikonomidis et al. , 2023 ), such as crop lodging, lack of
nutrition, diseases and pests, especially pests that do great harm to
crops (Liu and Wang, 2021). Pests that eat plants or lay eggs, destroy
the transfusion tissue of crops, prevent the transport of nutrients and
spread viruses, which will indirectly lead to crop malnutrition and
disease infection, resulting in lower crop yields and higher economic
losses. Because of the wide variety and huge quantity of crop pests, it
is inefficient to distinguish pests only by human eyes. When pests are
discovered, they have already spread over a large area around them.
Therefore, the intelligent automatic detection technology of pests is
especially essential for the improvement of agricultural productivity.
Accurate detection of pests can reduce the excessive use of pesticides,
increase crop yields and speed up the construction process of smart
agriculture.
With the persistent development and application of computer vision
technology, the degree of agriculture automation has been improved,

oping forward in an intelligent direction (Sivaranjani et al., 2022). For
instance, fine-grained visual categorization models ( Yu et al. , 2021b)
are employed in crop disease diagnosis ( Yu et al., 2022), cultivar vari-
eties recognition (Yu et al., 2021a), insect wing classification (Yu et al.,
2020); object detection models are used for cotton boll counting ( Liu
et al., 2023), precision weed control ( Ruigrok et al. , 2023), and field
pest detection (Ye et al., 2023) and so on. Computer vision provides a
new way for the intelligence of precision agriculture. At present, pest
detection research mostly concentrates on the identification of large
pests (Qi et al. , 2023; Freitas et al. , 2022; Chodey and Shariff , 2023;
Azfar et al., 2023), but in the actual field data collection process, due
to the influence of pest activity, actual pests often appear as small
objects in the images. Nevertheless, these techniques are designed to
identify pests in close-up images (e.g., IP102 Wu et al. , 2019), where
the pest covers the most portion of the image (see Fig. 1-a). They are not
suitable for processing real-world

One of the difficulties affecting the accuracy of field pest detection
is the effective detection of small pests, which belongs to the sub-
class of small object detection. Recently, general object detection has
developed rapidly and applied successfully in many fields, but small
object detection is still facing tough challenges (Kaur and Singh, 2022).
Due to the limitation of low resolution, small objects generate weaker
features than large objects after multi-layer convolution operation,
which leads to poor detection accuracy of small objects. The existing
small object detection solutions (Li et al., 2023b) focus on the effective
utilization of context information and the suitable design of neural
architectures. Context information utilization: Cui et al. (2022) design a
context-aware block network, which uses pyramid dilated convolution
to combine multi-layer context information without losing the original
resolution of the feature maps. Ji et al. ( 2023) propose a small object
detection algorithm, which introduces an expanded field-of-perception
block to obtain the object context features, and combines them with the
convolution features to obtain more robust and discriminant features.
Neural architecture design: Min et al. ( 2022) propose a novel feature
pyramid structure. The dynamic texture attention module highlights
the underlying small objects by filtering redundant semantics. Xiaolin
et al. (2022) propose the improved model. The original image and the
reduced image are fed into the detection network, and then the super-
resolution image enhancement module is proposed to enhance the
feature extraction of small objects. It appears that current small object
detection methods present a solution to address this issue, however, the
most of them still have the following two limitations: (1) These methods
are initially designed to detect common objects. when used for pest
detection, it is difficult for them to effectively capture and make full use
of plant context information in input images. The information usually
describes the external living environment of pests, such as the types
of crops and various plant organs. Therefore, it is helpful to enhance
the detection performance of small pests. (2) The network architectures
of most previous small object detection models are manually designed,
which are generally sub-optimal and eventually limit their applicability
in real-world field pest detection tasks.
As mentioned above, the use of context information and the design
of neural architecture are crucial for field pest detection. Therefore,
we propose the pest detection network (PestNAS) based on adaptive
feature fusion and evolutionary neural architecture search. For the
current situation of insufficient utilization of plant context information
for small pest detection, we design the two-branch backbone network
to extract plant features and pest features respectively, and adaptive
fusion of the two features by the exponential function to ensure the
effective use of context information. For the limitation of hand-crafted
pest detection architecture, we design the automatic design solution of
pest detection model based on evolutionary neural architecture search.
It mainly includes evolutionary search space and the GA-Adam search
algorithm. The evolutionary search space is composed of novel search
space and search space evolution mechanism, which can effectively
improve the feature expression of pests. On the basis of evolutionary
search space, the original gradient-based neural architecture search
tends to fall into local optimality, resulting in low accuracy of the
searched pest detection architecture. we design the GA-Adam algorithm
to improve the convergence ability of the original Adam algorithm
through selection, crossover and mutation strategies, so as to enhance
the search ability of the neural architecture. Our main contributions
can be summarized as follows:
• Since the ineffective utilization of background plant information
in field pest detection, we design the parallel backbone network
to extract plant features as context information for pest detection,
and we design the adaptive feature fusion method to effectively
integrate pest-related features and plant auxiliary features.
• For the problem that field pests are small in scale and difficult to
express their own features, we design the novel search space that
includes resolution and receptive field enhancement operations
to improve pest representation. The novel search space evolution
is designed by statistical operations and adaptive feature weight

2. Related work
2.1. Pest detection
At present, research on pest detection mainly focuses on the ap-
plications and lightweight of general object detection, dense object
detection, and small object detection (Teixeira et al., 2023). The ap-
plications and lightweight of general object detection: on the basis of
YOLOv5, Li et al. (2023a) add the attention module to focus on pests in
the channel and spatial dimension and improve the detection accuracy.
In addition, a new point-line distance loss function is presented to
reduce redundant calculation and shorten detection time. Yang et al.
(2023) apply the CSPResNeXt-50 module and VoVGSCSP module to im-
prove YOLOv7, and propose a new high-precision and real-time Maize
pest detection method, Maize-YOLO, which can enhance the accuracy
and speed of detection, reduce the computation of the model. Dense ob-
ject detection: Wen et al. (2022) propose a multi-species and dense pest
detector, named Pest-YOLO, and designs a non-intersection over Union
bounding box selection and suppression algorithm that can minimize
pest detection errors and omissions caused by occlusion, adhesion and
unlabeling between dense pest individuals. Du et al. (2022) propose a
new metric object density level to measure dense pest distribution in
images, using a pre-trained Cluster Region Proposal Network to select
suitable dense cluster areas of objects from the image. Then they are
classified into different groups by their density. Finally, cluster areas
with the same size and density are output to the detector to complete
the task of dense pest detection. Small object detection: Huang et al.
(2022) propose an adaptive small pest detection network based on the
CenterNet framework. The branches with learnable gating functions
are integrated into the trunk, and supervised learning is performed on
them. The learned gating function adaptively controls the combination
of these feature maps and the trunk to improve the detection effect
of small pests. Liu et al. (2022) construct a global activated feature
pyramid network on the backbone of the convolutional neural network
to detect small pests on a large scale at the location and pyramid level.
The network can retrieve different levels of depth and spatial intensity
information in the feature pyramid, which makes the changes of spatial
or depth-sensitive features in small pest images more visible. Due to
the fact that small object detection is one of the most critical issues
affecting the accuracy of field pest detection, this paper studies and
designs the novel search space from the perspective of small object
detection.
2.2. Neural architecture search
According to the different search mechanisms, the present neural
architecture search methods (Baymurzina et al., 2022) are mainly
divided into: based on reinforcement learning, based on evolutionary
algorithm, based on gradient method. Reinforcement learning: Lyu
et al. (2023) design a neural structure search scheme based on multi-
objective reinforcement learning. In order to balance resource cost
and performance, the scheme comprehensively considers accuracy, pa-
rameters, FLOPs and inference delay. Under different hyperparameter
configurations, the search process produces a set of excellent architec-
tures for efficient portrait parsing models. Han et al. (2022) propose
a neural network architecture search method based on reinforcement
learning RLNAS, which introduces block-based search and weight-
sharing mechanisms to reduce the computational cost. By optimizing
the multi-objective reward function to balance the tradeoff between
precision and computational efficiency, the final optimal structure is
obtained to realize the automatic architecture design in hyperspec-
tral unmixing. Evolutionary algorithm: Peng et al. (2023) propose a
new evolutionary neural architecture search strategy, predictor-assisted
evolutionary NAS, which utilizes a new evolutionary search strategy
and integrates high-quality weight inheritance between generations.
Different from the single strategy, the candidate offspring in PRE-NAS
are homogeneous in topology. This avoids bias and leads to more
accurate predictions that perform well even in a very small number
of assessment frameworks. Xue et al. (2023) propose a multi-objective
evolutionary algorithm based on probability stack, which considers
both accuracy and time consumption. MOEA-PS uses adjacency lists to
represent the internal structure of the deep neural network, introduces
a unique mechanism to guide the crossover and mutation process
of offspring, uses the surrogate model to stack structural blocks and
generates deep neural networks. Gradient method: Guo et al. (2022)
introduce a new structure parameterization method based on scaled
sigmoid function. For random supernet and conventional CNNs, a
novel channel-wise module is constructed. The network optimization is

3.3. The proposed approach—PestNAS
Fig. 2 shows the schematic diagram of field pest detection based
on adaptive feature fusion and evolutionary neural architecture search.
Our main contributions are adaptive feature fusion, novel search space,
search space evolution, and search algorithm–GA-Adam, represented
in red font in Fig. 2. The schematic diagram is analyzed as follows:
Firstly, the field pest dataset is labeled and trained according to the
plant category and the pest category respectively, and the pest-related
features and plant auxiliary features are adaptively fused. Then the
fused features are input into the feature pyramid network for feature
enhancement. The architectures and network parameters used in the
search process are shared among various levels of the feature pyramid
network. Since bounding box regression pays attention to local detail
information, object classification is achieved for features with more
semantic information (i.e. deeper feature maps). Therefore, bounding
box prediction is calculated from the output of the front cell, while
classification is performed on the output of the back cell. After that,
the neural architecture search part of the network is used for better
feature expression. we design the novel search space containing ten
operations for architecture selection, and mark the mutation by statis-
tical operation score, and apply the feature weight mutation method
to evolve the search space. Next, the GA-Adam algorithm optimizes
the objective function of the neural architecture search to select and
iterate the operations between nodes in the cell. At last, the neural
architecture with relatively optimal detection performance is used for
field pest detection.

assist in the identification of small pests. Therefore, we propose to use
a parallel backbone network module in the object detection network to
extract plant features as context information, then fuse plant features

Abstract—Hyperspectral unmixing (HU) based on autoen-
coders (AEs) is a crucial research task in remote sensing imagery.
While existing deep HU networks primarily focus on spatial
features, the inherently rich and continuous spectral bands in
hyperspectral images (HSIs) harbor signiﬁcant underutilized
information. The intrinsic characteristics of these continuous
bands can naturally enable more nuanced and eﬀective modeling
of mixed pixels. In this article, we propose the multiview collabo-
rative dual-branch network (MCDB-Net), designed to fully learn
and exploit the complex spectral features in high-dimensional
hyperspectral data, thereby enhancing the representation capa-
bilities of these features. MCDB-Net constructs a novel multiview
spectral block to strengthen the correlation between multiple
views of pixel spectra. The full-view spectral feature extraction
module highlights important spectral features, while the local
multiview spectral feature extraction module provides a detailed
understanding of the interactions between multiview spectral
information. The multiview abundance collaboration module
collaboratively learns spectral feature information from diﬀerent
perspectives and dynamically adjusts the weights of abundance
estimations, leading to better integration of abundance features
across various views. Extensive experiments on diﬀerent datasets
demonstrate that MCDB-Net achieves higher continuity and
robustness in unmixing results, showcasing its powerful capability
in spectral feature extraction.
Index Terms—Attention mechanism, autoencoder (AE), hyper-
spectral image (HSI), multiview learning, spectral unmixing.

increasing the number of spectral bands to hundreds or
thousands, thereby revealing intricate spectral details [1], [2].
However, the restricted spatial resolution often results in mixed
pixels composed of various ground materials. Hyperspectral

while supporting subsequent hyperspectral tasks [3]. This
work focuses on linear spectral unmixing (LMM), where
mixed pixel spectra are linearly combined to infer material
abundances, facilitating material classiﬁcation and quantitative

the ﬁrst is the abundance nonnegativity constraint (ANC); the
second is the abundance sum-to-one constraint (ASC) [4].
In this work, we mainly focus on the issue of LMM.
This includes traditional linear unmixing methods based on
geometry, statistics, and sparse regression, as well as HU
methods based on deep learning that have been widely used in
recent years. There are mainly two types of HU methods based
on geometry: methods based on the pure pixel assumption and
methods based on minimum volume (MV). For the unmixing
algorithms based on pure pixels, representative algorithms
include the vertex component analysis (VCA) [5], the simplex
growing algorithm (SGA) [6], and N-FINDR [7]. The fully
constrained least squares (FCLSs) algorithm [4] relies on
the extracted endmember information to further accurately
calculate and obtain the abundance information. However, in
practical situations, there are few cases that satisfy the pure
pixel assumption, which greatly increases the complexity and
challenge of HU. To handle highly mixed HSI, a more eﬃcient

the relationship between the abundance vectors corresponding

to explore the abundant spatial and spectral features contained
in HSI more comprehensively and deeply, a series of weighted
sparse unmixing algorithms have been continuously developed
[26], [27], [28], [29], [30]. These algorithms are committed to
improving the utilization eﬃciency of spatial–spectral features,
optimizing the unmixing models from diﬀerent perspectives
and aspects, and ﬁnally achieving the goal of enhancing the
unmixing results.
Over the past few years, deep learning has been widely
applied in HU, driving the development of HU. In the
autoencoder (AE) network structure, the encoder reduces the
dimension of the input data to generate abundance fractions.
The weights of the decoder are regarded as endmembers, and
meanwhile, pixels are recreated based on the obtained abun-
dances. Typical examples constructed based on this framework
include uDAS [31], DAEN [32], MTAEU [33], EndNet [34],
TANet [35], SSRDMF [36], DASS-Net [37], A2SAN [38],
SSABN [39], RTViT-Net [40], MAT-Net [41], and SSLT-Net
[42]. uDAS adopts denoising constraints to avoid introduc-
ing additional denoising errors and uses l2,1 constraints to
reduce the redundancy of the encoder, thus lowering the
reconstruction error. DAEN employs a stacked AE (SAE)
to learn spectral features, generating a better initialization
for the unmixing process. It uses a variational AE (V AE)
for blind signal separation to obtain both endmembers and
abundances simultaneously. MTAEU uses multitask learning
to train multiple AEs in parallel to simultaneously decompose
the neighborhoods of pixels, thereby alleviating the impact of
endmember translation variability. EndNet eﬀectively applies
sparsity and nonlinearity by correcting the ReLU activation
function and the normalization layer, and proposes a new
loss function to enhance sparsity. TANet adopts two AEs
that share the same weights to extract physically meaning-
ful endmembers. SSRDMF reduces the impact of Gaussian
noise and sparse noise by explicitly modeling sparse noise
and introducing self-supervised constraints to explore spectral
information. DASS-Net explores spatial information by lever-
aging neighborhood attention and fuses spatial and spectral
features to improve the accuracy of endmember extraction
and abundance estimation. Tao et al. [38] propose the A2SN
and A2SAN networks. Through innovative unmixing strate-
gies, embedding attention mechanisms, and introducing an
abundance guidance mechanism, these networks can directly
extract endmembers from the network, estimate abundances,
and reconstruct images, enhancing the robustness against
noise. Yang et al. [39] construct the spatial–spectral attention
bilateral network. By utilizing Swin transformer blocks and
a simpliﬁed spectral channel attention mechanism to extract
and fuse spatial and spectral information, respectively, the
performance of HU is improved. Shu et al. [40] develop
the RTViT-Net speciﬁcally for HU, integrating an innovative
token generation mechanism into its design. To address the
limitations of single-scale feature extraction in HU, Wang
et al. [41] propose the MAT-Net, which achieves spectral
and multiscale spatial feature fusion through a dual-stream
multibranch encoder and a customized transformer encoder.
Deng et al. [42] introduce SSLT-Net, a hybrid model that
combines a convolutional neural network (CNN) and a linear
transformer, to realize the optimized fusion of local, global,
spatial, and spectral features for HU tasks.
In the ﬁeld of HU, CNNs have emerged as a high-
performance network architecture due to their remarkable
local perception capability and superior ability to extract
spatial–spectral features [43], while transformers have also
been widely applied by virtue of their advantages in global
feature modeling. Palsson et al. [44] directly explore the
spatial correlations of HSI through CNN and propose a
novel spatial–spectral linear mixing model, which simpliﬁes
the application of spatial regularization. Gao et al. [45]
propose a cycle-consistent unmixing network. By relaxing
the original pixel-level reconstruction assumption and impos-
ing cycle-consistency constraints, they transfer high-level
semantic information in

In contrast to conventional band selection approaches, spec-
tral partitioning does not simply select a part of the bands.
Instead, it utilizes the whole set of spectral bands to provide
multiview data for subsequent image processing by generating
multiple views of the HSI. Spectral partitioning divides the
spectral bands into multiple highly correlated subsets [51], and
regenerates subsamples of the original spectral bands from the
obtained spectral clusters. A multitude of spectral partitioning
methods exist in the realm of HSI classiﬁcation. Notable
examples include the methods described in[52], [53], [54], and
[55]. In [52], a spectrometer-driven (SD) classiﬁcation strategy
for HSI is proposed. It is based on a full understanding of the
working principle of spectrometers and the physical character-
istics of imaging spectrometers to improve the classiﬁcation
capabilities. In [54], adaptive aﬃnity propagation (AAP) [56]
is adopted to automatically select the number of clusters
and centering parameters through unsupervised clustering, and
reassign the partitions into new band groups. Similarly, there
are applications in the ﬁeld of unmixing. RMSU [57] is a
spatial–spectral multiview data generation approach that per-
forms multiview dictionary learning and estimates abundances
based on a joint dictionary. In addition, Qi et al. [58] propose
the spectral–spatial-weighted multiview collaborative sparse
unmixing method to make full use of spectral and spatial
information and improve the unmixing performance. This
marks the ﬁrst proposal of the multiview unmixing concept
in the ﬁeld of HU. Experimental validation has revealed that
abundance estimates from di ﬀerent views exhibit signiﬁcant
discrepancies, which can be eﬀectively harnessed to enhance
the accuracy of abundance estimation. Based on this ﬁnding,
Qi et al. [59] further introduce the signiﬁcant discovery of
multiview strategies into the AE-based unmixing framework
and propose a multiview spatial–spectral two-stream network.
By designing two AEs and leveraging recurrent neural net-
works (RNNs), they achieve the collaborative utilization of
multiview spectral–spatial information, enabling the unmixing
process to more meticulously explore the potential value of
multidimensional spectral feature information.
In summary, most of the existing HU methods extract
spectral features from a single perspective of mixed pixels,
which severely restricts the eﬀective capture of deep spectral
features. As a result, when faced with complex land object
scenes, it is diﬃcult to accurately analyze the rich spectral
feature information contained in hyperspectral data, especially
in the obvious deﬁciency of modeling complex spectral inter-
actions. Following the development of multiview unmixing,
this study focuses on the in-depth mining of spectral features
in hyperspectral data and the eﬃcient integration of multiview
information, and is committed to improving the performance
of multiview unmixing. In the unmixing model based on
the AE, a novel multiview spectral construction method is
innovatively introduced to fully unleash the technical potential
of multiview unmixing. This method divides the spectral bands
from multiple views and skillfully combines them into spectral
blocks, enabling the constructed model to comprehensively
and deeply utilize complex spectral interactions, thus pro-
viding a brand-new idea for HU. Based on this, this article
proposes an HU model called multiview collaborative dual-
branch network (MCDB-Net) based on multiview abundance
collaboration. This model is expected to signiﬁcantly improve
the accuracy and robustness of HU. The main contributions of
this study are as follows.
1) To break through the limitation that traditional HU
methods over-rely on a single view and fail to fully
excavate spectral features, a novel multiview unmixing
learning framework based on single-pixel expansion is
proposed. Abandoning the analytical mode of isolated
single-pixel spectra, this framework innovatively trans-
forms individual pixel spectra into multidimensional
spectral combinations by constructing multiview spectral
blocks, realizing a leap from single-point feature extrac-
tion to multidimensional feature collaborative capture. It
provides a new idea for the thorough mining of spectral
information in complex mixed ground object scenar-
ios, signiﬁcantly enhances the model’s adaptability to
complex mixed spectra, and lays a solid foundation for
accurate unmixing.
2) To eﬃciently integrate the global and local multiview
spectral information, a dual-branch multiview network
structure is adopted. The global branch comprehensively
captures the overall spectral features of hyperspectral
data through a full-view attention mechanism, suppress-
ing unimportant spectral bands and highlighting key
spectral features. The local branch generates multiple

information interaction under multiple views, integrate global

Multitask Hyperspectral Classiﬁcation
Network With Unmixing Assistance

Abstract—Multitask learning (MTL) can eﬀectively exploit the
complementary information across diﬀerent tasks in hyperspec-
tral images (HSIs) to support classiﬁcation. However, existing
MTL methods for HSI classiﬁcation usually employ shared
structures in the early stages or simple information fusion in
the later stages, failing to adequately characterize task-speciﬁc
feature diﬀerences and adaptively select task-relevant informa-
tion. Therefore, we propose a multistage information sharing
multitask hyperspectral classiﬁcation network with unmixing
assistance (MSUANet). The proposed method adopts a three-stage
strategy, including low-level information sharing, task-speciﬁc
information mining, and adaptive latent information selection,
to fully exploit the information gain introduced by the unmix-
ing task and provide more ﬁne-grained spectral details for
improved classiﬁcation performance. In addition, we propose
an information diverter with hybrid attention (IDHA) module,
which enhances task-speciﬁc information for classiﬁcation and
unmixing, respectively. Furthermore, we design the adaptive
latent abundance knowledge transfer (ALAKT) module, which
adaptively selects latent complementary information for both
tasks. The experimental results on Indian Pines, Houston 2013,
Berlin, and Washington DC MALL datasets demonstrate that
MSUANet outperforms state-of-the-art methods. The source code
will be available at https://github.com/chihuajiao/HSIMTL
Index Terms—Deep learning (DL), hyperspectral image (HSI)
classiﬁcation, hyperspectral unmixing, multitask learning (MTL).

I. I NTRODUCTION
R
EMOTE sensing technology [1] has advanced rapidly in
recent years, which has signiﬁcantly enhanced both the
spatial and spectral resolution of earth surface observations.
Compared with optical remote sensing imagery, hyperspec-
tral images (HSIs) acquire hundreds of contiguous spectral
bands covering the ultraviolet to infrared regions, providing
substantially richer spectral information. HSIs are widely used
in agricultural monitoring [2], [3], urban planning [4], [5],
land-cover survey [6], and target recognition [7].
Over the past few decades, HSI classiﬁcation has been a
fundamental task in hyperspectral data analysis. Traditional
approaches have primarily relied on manually designed feature
extraction methods [8], [9], [10] combined with machine
learning algorithms [11], [12]. Although these traditional
approaches achieved notable success, their heavy dependence
on handcrafted features and expert knowledge severely lim-
its their generalization capabilities across diverse scenarios.
Deep learning (DL) methods can learn features from raw
data automatically, which eﬀectively overcomes the limita-
tions of manual feature extraction [13], [14]. Early research
focused on spectral feature extraction networks [15], [16] and
spatial feature extraction networks [17], [18], extracting deep-
level spatial and spectral representations through convolutional
neural networks (CNNs). However, this separate extraction
method may overlook the complex relationships between
spectral and spatial information. Subsequently, researchers
have considered e
