constrained to a single-task learning paradigm. This isolated
strategy fails to exploit the potential synergies among diﬀerent
tasks [27], [28] in HSI analysis. In fact, HSIs contain rich
semantic information that must be interpreted from multiple
task perspectives. For instance, HSI super-resolution focuses
on mining subpixel spectral and spatial details [29], [30]. HSI
sharpening emphasizes the enhancement of object boundary
clarity [31]. HSI reconstruction aims to recover low noise
and low interference spectral and spatial representations [32],
and HSI unmixing is dedicated to estimating the constituent
material abundances at the subpixel level [33], [34]. These
tasks can provide complementary information to support clas-
siﬁcation from various dimensions. Nevertheless, eﬃciently
sharing knowledge and features across these tasks remains a
signiﬁcant challenge.
Multitask learning (MTL) is a learning paradigm in
which multiple related tasks [35] are trained jointly. By
leveraging shared representations and cross-task knowl-
edge transfer, MTL can eﬀectively capture and exploit
the latent relationships among tasks [36], [37]. In recent
years, several studies have introduced MTL into the HSI
domain and proposed various types of parameter sharing
strategies. Some studies adopt a hard parameter sharing
mechanism [38], [39] by constructing a backbone network that
handles HSI classiﬁcation and other HSI tasks simultaneously.
Those methods have a simple structure and can automatically
learn representations common to multiple tasks. However,
since all tasks share the same parameters, it lacks the ability
to model the diﬀerences between tasks, which is prone to
causing interference between tasks. Other studies adopt a
soft parameter sharing mechanism [40], [41] by designing
a distinct subnetwork for each task and facilitating informa-
tion sharing through an attention mechanism. For instance,
Han et al. [42] proposed a two-branch network for unmixing
and classiﬁcation that delivers abundance information to the
classiﬁcation task via attention, thereby strengthening the
cross-task semantic connection. While soft parameter sharing
captures task-speciﬁc features well, its separate subnetworks
limit eﬃcient information sharing. To combine the advan-
tages of both, some scholars have adopted a hybrid sharing
mechanism. For instance, HyMuT [43] has achieved excellent
performance on multiple datasets by constructing a shared
backbone network and a hierarchical information transfer
mechanism. However, this structure lacks the dynamic per-
ception of task information, and it is diﬃcult to adaptively
meet task-speciﬁc requirements. In general, existing hyper-
spectral MTL methods can leverage auxiliary tasks to bring
performance gains to classiﬁcation. However, their sharing
mechanisms are generally basic and lack task-speciﬁc design,
failing to eﬀectively exploit the potential complementary infor-
mation and deeper correlations among diﬀerent tasks.
To address these limitations, we propose a multistage infor-
mation sharing multitask hyperspectral classiﬁcation network
with unmixing assistance (MSUANet). The proposed network
employs a multistage sharing mechanism to deeply extract
both shared and task-speciﬁc features from the classiﬁcation
and unmixing branches. Furthermore, it performs targeted
information ﬁltering tailored to the characteristics of the
classiﬁcation task, thereby enhancing the performance of HSI
classiﬁcation. MSUANet comprises three stages of informa-
tion sharing. First, a shared backbone network is constructed
to extract common features across tasks. Based on this, to
mitigate mutual interference among tasks, we introduce an
information diverter with hybrid attention (IDHA) module
in the decoding stage to generate task-speciﬁc feature rep-
resentations. Finally, we propose an adaptive latent abundance
knowledge transfer (ALAKT) module, which dynamically
perceives the importance of information generated by both
classiﬁcation and unmixing decoders. This module adaptively
ﬁlters eﬀective features for the classiﬁcation task. As shown in
Fig. 1, MSUANet leverages a multistage information sharing
mechanism to make the feature activation regions of the
classiﬁcation task more focused on the true target areas,
while more eﬀectively exploiting the potential beneﬁts pro-
vided by the auxiliary task. In brief, our contributions are as
follows.
1) We propose an MSUANet. The network integrates
shared representation learning, task-speciﬁc modeling,
and adaptive information selection

The remainder of this article is organized as follows. In
Section II, we introduce the relevant background knowledge
of MTL and HSI unmixing tasks and the motivation of
MSUANet. In Section III, we elaborate on the proposed
MSUANet architecture in detail. In Section IV, we validate
the proposed MSUANet through experiments conducted on
four HSI datasets. The evaluation includes ablation studies,
comparisons with state-of-the-art methods. Finally, Section V
concludes this article and outlines potential directions for
future research.
II. B ACKGROUND AND MOTIVATION
A. Multitask Learning

individual models separately. It captures shared representations
among tasks while preserving task-speciﬁc characteristics,
thereby improving generalization performance across tasks.
The objective of MTL is to minimize the total loss across all
tasks, combining both task-speciﬁc losses and a regularization
term on the model parameters. For T tasks, let θs denote the
shared parameters and θ j denote the task-speciﬁc parameters

Recently, many researchers have introduced MTL into HSI
classiﬁcation by leveraging auxiliary tasks such as superpixel
modeling [44], [45], spectral reconstruction [46], and domain
adaptation [47], among others. These auxiliary tasks provide
useful prior information, enabling the model to improve its
representation learning and thus better support the primary
classiﬁcation task. For instance, Li et al. [48] introduced
a graph-based sample relationship learning task, optimizing
sample distances in the feature space via a Siamese network,
eﬀectively mitigating the overﬁtting problem in few-shot HSI
classiﬁcation. Liu et al.[49] proposed a spectral reconstruction
auxiliary task, which uses reconstruction errors to detect and
identify unknown classes, signiﬁcantly enhancing the general-
ization capability of the HSI classiﬁer in open-world scenarios.
Chen et al. [50] developed a cross-domain contrastive learning
task, aligning cross-domain samples in the feature space to
facilitate the transfer of knowledge from the source domain to
the target domain, thereby signiﬁcantly improving the accuracy
of HSI classiﬁcation across diverse scenes.
Most existing methods enhance feature representation by
directly fusing information from auxiliary tasks. However,
this naive aggregation strategy often overlooks the correla-
tions between tasks and lacks an eﬀective mechanism for
selecting useful information. Consequently, it may introduce
redundant or even conﬂicting information [51], diminishing
the beneﬁts of auxiliary tasks. We propose a multistage sharing
strategy that combines low-level feature sharing, mining of
task-speciﬁc representations, and adaptive selection of task-
relevant information, fully leveraging the potential of auxiliary
tasks to achieve more eﬀective MTL.
B. HSI Unmixing

from mixed pixels due to limited spatial resolution. HSI
unmixing decomposes these pixels into endmembers and abun-

model (LMM) and nonlinear unmixing model (NLMM) based
on the mixing mechanisms of endmembers within a pixel.
Under the LMM, the spectral signature of each component
combines in a linearly proportional manner. In contrast,
NLMM accounts for complex interactions between endmem-
bers, resulting in mixed spectra that cannot be accurately
represented through linear combinations. Here, we focus on

unmixing not only oﬀers physically interpretable spectral
representations but also provides spatial priors that can yield
additional information gain for other tasks. Motivated by this
beneﬁt, we adopt unmixing as an auxiliary task and employ
a multistage information sharing strategy to fully exploit its
potential in enhancing HSI classiﬁcation performance.
C. Task-Speciﬁc Attention for HSI
In recent years, attention mechanisms have been widely
applied in the ﬁeld of HSI analysis. The core idea is to
adaptively assign feature weights to emphasize discrimina-
tive information while suppressing redundant features. Early
studies mainly embedded spatial and spectral attention into
CNNs [58], [59] to enhance discriminative feature responses.
Wu et al. [60] employed a dual-branch 3-D CNN to separately
capture spatial and spectral attention features of HSIs, thereby
achieving collaborative enhancement at the feature level.
Li et al. [61] integrated the squeeze and excitation attention
[62] with multiscale convolutions to realize adaptive recalibra-
tion of spatial and spectral hierarchical features. Chen et al.
[63] incorporated the convolutional block attention [64] into
CNNs, jointly modeling channel and spatial attention to further
improve classiﬁcation performance. With the rise of self-
attention mechanisms [65], [66], Hong et al. [67] proposed
SpectralFormer, which revisits HSI classiﬁcation through spec-
tral sequence modeling. By learning local dependencies among
adjacent spectral bands and employing cross-layer skip con-
nections, SpectralFormer enables adaptive fusion of multilevel
features. Sun et al. [68] introduced SSFTT, which tokenizes
spectral and spatial features separately before feeding them
into a Transformer encoder, capturing high-order semantic
relationships and signiﬁcantly improving classiﬁcation accu-
racy. Subsequently, HyperTransformer [69] fuses spectral and
texture information across multiple spatial scales and models
cross-modal feature dependencies to enhance representation
capability.
Overall, these attention mechanisms have made signiﬁ-
cant progress in spatial spectral feature modeling. However,
in hyperspectral MTL, there is a lack of exclusive feature
enhancement for each task, making it diﬃcult to screen rele-
vant and irrelevant features for each task, which leads to the
introduction of redundant and confusing information. Inspired
by the self-attention mechanism, we propose the IDHA, which
performs task-speciﬁc feature modeling to capture the task
of exclusive information, reduce feature interference, and
improve the overall expressiveness of the learned represen-
tations.
III. M ETHODOLOGY
MSUANet is designed to fully exploit the potential beneﬁts
of auxiliary tasks for the main classiﬁcation task through
a multistage information sharing strategy. As illustrated in
Fig. 2, the framework consists of three information sharing
stages and one task head stage. In the information shar-
ing phase, the model sequentially performs shared feature
extraction, task-speciﬁc information enhancement, and adap-
tive information selection, thereby progressively extracting and
reﬁning useful representations for each task. Subsequently,
the processed information is delivered to their respective task
processing modules. The following will provide a detailed
description of the multistage sharing mechanism in MSUANet
and the corresponding improvements applied to the stages.
A. Multistage Sharing Mechanism
The multistage sharing mechanism of MSUANet is
shown in Fig. 2. This mechanism mainly consists of three
stages: shared feature extraction, task-speciﬁc information
enhancement, and adaptive information selection.
1) Shared Feature Extraction Stage: In the ﬁrst stage, a
uniﬁed feature encoder extracts deep representations from HSI,

SHMD: A Sequential Approach for Martian Hydrated
Minerals Detection and Abundance Mapping
Sicong Liu , Senior Member , IEEE, Bo Wan, Xuanning Lu, Lu Lu, Y usheng Xu , Member , IEEE,
Xiaohua Tong , Fellow, IEEE,H u a nX i e , Senior Member , IEEE, Y ongjiu Feng ,Y a n m i nJ i n,
and Paolo Gamba , Fellow, IEEE
Abstract—Hydrated minerals (HMs) serve as key indicators of
geological processes and the historical presence of water on Mars.
Detecting their distribution and composition via remote sensing
is therefore crucial for advancing our understanding of Martian
aqueous environments. Current detection approaches typically rely
on predeﬁned spectral libraries or endmembers extracted directly
from images, often overlooking signals from low-abundance com-
ponents. This leads to low automation in the detection process
and unstable inversion results for HM identiﬁcation. To address
these limitations, we propose a novel framework named sequen-
tial hydrated mineral detection (SHMD). This method adaptively
extracts endmembers from distinct regions using qualitative data
without requiring prior information. An automated endmember
extraction process further ensures the accuracy and precision of
the HM inversion. In this study, experiments were conducted within
three regions of the Perseverance rover’s candidate landing site.
Four categories of samples were labeled in Mawrth Vallis data, and
classiﬁcation accuracy was evaluated using a HM abundance map.
Comparative experiments demonstrate that the proposed SHMD
outperforms the state-of-the-art methods in terms of detection
accuracy, particularly in regions with medium and low abundance
of HMs.
Index Terms —Abundance, endmember extraction, hydrated
minerals (HMs), hyperspectral, inversion, target detection,
unmixing.

life forms, plays a pivotal role in this exploration [1]. Although
stable liquid water is absent on Mars, water persists primarily as
ice and within hydrated minerals (HMs), such as clay minerals,
sulfates, and hydrated silica [1], [2]. Identifying these HMs is
crucial for understanding the potential for life, unraveling the
Martian geological history, and evaluating the planet’s suitability
for future exploration and settlement. HM signatures, and its oc-
currence with surrounding landforms and geomorphic features,
have signiﬁcantly guided landing sites selection [3], [4], [5].
For instance, Gale Crater was selected for the Curiosity rover
mission partly due to abundant phyllosilicates in the surrounding
region [6], indicating past aqueous activity [7]. HMs were also
detected around Mount Sharp within the crater [8]. Conse-
quently, Gale Crater emerged as the optimal candidate among
numerous landing sites [9]. Therefore, investigating the types
and spatial distribution of Martian surface minerals, particularly
hydrated phases, provides valuable insights for selecting future
Mars sample return mission sites. China’s Tianwen-3 mission,
which aims to return samples from the Martian surface, would
beneﬁt signiﬁcantly from such investigations. HMs not only
record past aqueous processes, but also preserve biosignatures
and provide crucial insights into the planet’s habitability [10].
Rover obtains accurate mineral composition information
through in situ detection. The Mars Surface Composition De-
tector (MarSCoD

1024 IEEE JOURNAL OF SELECTED TOPICS IN APPLIED EARTH OBSERV ATIONS AND REMOTE SENSING, VOL. 19, 2026
including spectral matching, spectral parameter analysis, and
target detection techniques[18], [19], [20], [21]. Spectral match-
ing, commonly used for large-scale detection, rapidly identiﬁes
speciﬁc minerals by comparing the absorption features between
the image spectra and the reference spectra [18]. However,
because of its limited accuracy, this method primarily provides
an overview of the large-scale distribution of HMs. For instance,
Christensen et al. [22] identiﬁed mineralogical evidence of po-
tential aqueous interactions in the Sinus Meridiani region using
spectral matching results from Thermal Emission Spectrometer
(TES) data.
Spectral parameter analysis has gained prominence for min-
eral characterization. Parameters such as BD1900 reﬂect hy-
dration characteristics, while OLINDEX indicates the presence
of olivine [19]. Numerous other spectral parameters have been
developed to capture diagnostic spectral features of speciﬁc min-
erals. Using data from Observatoire Mineralogie, Eau, Glaces,
Activite (OMEGA), Poulet [23] and Ody [24] mapped the global
distribution of HMs by calculating parameters indicative of the
water content. Similarly, Horgan et al. [25] used false-color
compositions of multiple parameters of spectral characteristics
at Jezero Crater (Perseverance’s landing site) to analyze the
characteristics of silicate and carbonate. Gou et al. Integrated
three spectral parameters (BD2210, BD1900, and OLINDEX)
from Compact Reconnaissance Imaging Spectrometer for Mars
(CRISM) data to identify HMs in Mawrth V allis, helping to
explain the diversity of phyllosilicates and alteration intensities
in the region [26]. Furthermore, Carter et al. [20] established the
Mars Orbital Catalog of Aqueous Alteration Signatures (MO-
CAAS) database, compiling global maps of aqueous secondary
minerals by identifying diagnostic spectral features in OMEGA
and CRISM data.
Although the spectral parameter method effectively captures
broad mineral characteristics, it exhibits lower accuracy in iden-
tifying speciﬁc mineral types due to its failure to incorporate
global spectral information. In contrast, target detection algo-
rithms employ mathematical processing of the spectral matrix,
enabling precise identiﬁcation of speciﬁc minerals at the pixel
level. Wu et al. [27] evaluated several target detection methods,
including Constrained Energy Minimization (CEM), Matched
ﬁlter (MF), and Multi-task Joint Sparse and low-rank Represen-
tation (MTJLSR), by mixing varying proportions of HMs with
simulated Martian soil (Mars global simulant, MGS-1) to assess
the detection ability of different HMs. Similarly, Lin et al. [21]
detected serpentine in Jezero Crater using an improved Factor
Analysis and Target Transformation(FA TT) method, which also
identiﬁed magnesite and serpentine in Nili Fossae.
Qualitative analysis can identify speciﬁc minerals but can-
not reveal their precise compositional information. To over-
come this limitation, hyperspectral quantitative inversion tech-
niques have been developed, typically involving two key pro-
cesses: endmember selection and spectral unmixing. The most
common approach for endmember selection utilizes a spectral
library composed of laboratory-measured spectra of pure min-
erals. However, this method highly relies on a priori knowl-
edge or expert experience, particularly when the speciﬁc types
of minerals present are unknown during library construction.
This reliance can introduce instability and subjectivity into
unmixing results. To address this issue, endmembers can be
directly extracted from hyperspectral imagery, offering a more
robust and automated alternative to traditional spectral libraries.
Ke et al. [28] categorized endmember detection methods into
pixel-based and subpixel-based approaches, emphasizing the ad-
vantages of spectral unmixing—particularly fully autonomous
unmixing—for regions with unknown mineral compositions.
Their comparison using synthetic and real CRISM data demon-
strated that spectral unmixing is more suitable for complex
mineral mixtures. Building on this, Wang et al. [29]
proposed
Saliency-based Autonomous Endmember Detection (SAED) to
extract stable endmembers. Nevertheless, the automated end-
member extraction process for Martian hyperspectral images
(HSIs) remains susceptible to noise interference.
The linear unmixing model remains the most widely used ap-
proach in spectral unmixing. Analysis of TES data on light-toned
units by Michalski and Fergason [30] revealed phyllosilicate
abundances of approximately 10%–20%, near TES detectability
thresholds. Viviano and Moersch [31] subsequently employed
multispectral data from the Thermal Emission Imaging Sys-
tem (THEMIS) to map phyllosilicate abundance distribution
in Mawrth V allis, identifying a maximum abundance of 63%.
Furthermore, various improved methods based on linear un-
mixing methods have

Martian HMs typically exhibit low abundance and dispersed
spatial distributions, often occurring alongside uncertain or
unidentiﬁed background minerals. Furthermore, factors such
as nonlinear spectral mixing, instrumental noise, and spectral
variability further complicate their detection. These challenges
pose signiﬁcant obstacles to the accurate identiﬁcation and
quantitative inversion of Martian HMs. This study addresses
these challenges by investigating advanced methods for mineral
identiﬁcation and quantitative inversion using hyperspectral re-
mote sensing data. The purpose is to achieve a more accurate
assessment of the spatial distribution and abundance of HMs.
To this end, a novel detection framework integrating qualitative
identiﬁcation and quantitative inversion methods is proposed,
offering the following advantages.
1) It ﬁrst employs target detection results to construct pre-
liminary geological information, which is subsequently
integrated into a quantitative spectral unmixing model.
This fully automated approach eliminates the dependence
on expert a priori knowledge.
2) Endmembers are extracted speciﬁcally from the detection
results of HMs, rather than from the entire image. This
targeted strategy mitigates the omission of low-abundance
minerals and enables direct classiﬁcation of the extracted
endmembers.
3) An automated mineral endmember inspection (AMEI)
procedure is introduced to identify and eliminate incor-
rectly extracted endmembers, thereby enhancing the reli-
ability and accuracy of the spectral unmixing results.
The rest of this article is organized as follows: Section II pro-
vides a detailed description of the proposed method. Section III
introduces the study region and the data used. Section IV
presents an analysis of the qualitative and quantitative detection
results of HMs, evaluates the abundance unmixing performance,
and analyzes representative HM distribution results along with
terrain data within the study region. Finally, SectionV concludes
this article.
II. P
ROPOSED FRAMEWORK
This work aims to develop an automatic and reliable tech-
nique to detect HMs without relying on any prior knowledge
or ground reference data. The technical framework, illustrated
in Fig. 1, consists of four stages: 1) data preprocessing; 2)
target-guided high-conﬁdence HM distribution region construc-
tion; 3) knowledge-driven endmember automatic inspection;
and 4) abundance mapping. Details are provided in the following
sections.
A. Data Preprocessing
Preprocessing includes correcting reﬂectance differences
caused by variations in solar elevation angle, applying atmo-
spheric correction using an empirical transmission function to
remove the spectral effects of the Martian atmosphere, and per-
forming georeferencing [33]. Furthermore, the process involves
removing noisy spectral bands and performing CoTCA T[34] to
reduce spectral noise.

Abstract
Over the past two decades, hyperspectral imaging (HSI) systems have shown significant
potential in agriculture, from disease detection to the assessment of plant and fruit nutri-
tional status. However, most applications remain confined to laboratory analyses under
controlled conditions, with only a limited fraction implemented in field environments. In
this scenario, spectral reconstruction techniques may serve as a bridge between the high
accuracy of HSI and the challenges of on-field or even real-time applications. This review
outlines the current state of the art of on-field HSI in the agrifood sector, highlighting
existing limitations and potential advantages. It then introduces the problem of spectral
reconstruction and reviews current techniques used to address it. Laboratory and on-field
studies will be taken into account. The final section offers our perspective on the limitations
of HSI and the promising potential of spectral super-resolution to overcome current barriers
and enable broader adoption of hyperspectral technology in precision agriculture.
Keywords: spectral super-resolution; multispecral imaging; hyperspectral imaging; deep
learning; proximal sensing
1. Introduction
Spectral reconstruction from RGB images—that is, generating multispectral or hyper-
spectral images from simple three-channel images (red, green, and blue)—is a topic that has
received increasing attention in the last decade. Native hyperspectral images, acquired with
hyperspectral cameras, provide richer information than traditional RGB images, capturing
data across multiple narrow spectral bands, from tens to hundreds of bands. It allows for
detecting chemical and physical properties in targets on the scene, related to the spectral
signature, without any damage or invasive sampling. This capability enables advanced
applications in various sectors, including remote sensing, agriculture, geology, medicine,
environmental monitoring, and cultural heritage preservation [1]. Within environmental
monitoring, air pollution is a topic where hyperspectral images are the best source of
information. However, hyperspectral cameras are generally complex, expensive, and often
impractical for large-scale applications or consumer contexts. To overcome these limita-
tions, a line of research has developed aimed at reconstructing detailed spectral information
from RGB images by leveraging advanced computational techniques and machine learning
models [2]. Generally, the reconstruction of hyperspectral images from RGB images is a
complex challenge due to information loss and limitations in data quality. First of all, there
Appl. Sci. 2025, 15, 10985 https://doi.org/10.3390/app152010985

Appl. Sci. 2025, 15, 10985 2 of 30
are problems of the non-uniqueness of the solution: reconstructing the spectrum from an
RGB image is not unique, as different spectral distributions can correspond to the same
RGB values. Given the sensor response, multiple input spectra can lead to identical integral
values. Moreover, there is lack of an RGB camera frequency response. So, we do not know
exactly how the camera works with the incoming spectrum. An important aspect of this
problem is that many models require knowledge of the spectral response of the sensor
(e.g. attention-block models) [ 1], which are not available for common RGB cameras. In
addition, we must couple with data degradation. Raw image values contain unknown pixel
responses directly related to the incoming electromagnetic waves, but JPEG compression,
white balance, and gamma correction degrade the original spectral information. However,
recent studies (from regression models to deep learning models) demonstrate promising
results, including predictions of spectral information beyond the visible spectrum, such as
in the NIR (near-infrared) region. The methods proposed in the literature can primarily
be divided into two general categories: prior-based methods and data-driven methods.
Prior-based methods exploit statistical information and spatial or spectral characteristics,
such as sparsity or spectral correlation [1]. On the other hand, data-driven methods mainly
rely on deep neural networks, which have demonstrated a great ability to model com-
plex relationships between RGB data and corresponding spectral information [3]. Recent
research has significantly focused on the use of deep learning techniques to address the
problem of spectral reconstruction. Approaches based on deep convolutional neural net-
works (CNNs), as well as more advanced architectures, such as Generative Adversarial
Networks (GANs), have shown remarkable effectiveness, especially when trained on large
datasets [1]. A critical issue in this field concerns the physical accuracy of reconstructed
images. Many current methods, although achieving good spectral accuracy, may generate
results that do not respect physical plausibility—meaning that reconstructed images do
not precisely yield the original RGB values when reintegrated with the camera’s spectral
sensitivities. To address this challenge, recent studies have developed physically plausible
reconstruction methods, introducing constraints based on the decomposition of spectral
information into fundamental metameric components. This allows for a reconstruction that
is physically coherent and robust to exposure variations [4]. A further advancement in re-
search involves the introduction of category-specific prior information—additional details
describing particular object types or surfaces present in the images—to further improve
reconstruction quality [5]. Finally, an important driver for developing these approaches
has been the creation of new datasets, such as ARAD-HS [6], which offers a wide variety of
natural hyperspectral images. These datasets enable rigorous validation and performance
comparisons among the various developed methods [7]. It is important to note that in the
analyzed studies, RGB and hyperspectral images can be treated either as directly measured
luminance data or as reflectance data, where the acquired signal is normalized against
the light source and environmental conditions. However, it should be emphasized that
many commonly cited datasets, such as ARAD-HS, CAVE, ICVL, and BGU-HS [1], do not
provide detailed calibration procedures for precise conversion to reflectance, one of the
most important steps in order to extract numerical information from the images related
to the status of plant and fruits. The only dataset explicitly described with rigorous cali-
bration via a standard white panel is the KAUST-HS dataset [1,6]. Consequently, the use
of reflectance data in studies based on these datasets should be approached cautiously,
recognizing potential limitations in their accuracy and generalizability. Applying these
models to images acquired under uncontrolled conditions remains an open challenge but
represents a significant area of research for food-quality analysis and other natural material
assessments. This study presents a detailed analysis of the topics previously introduced,
beginning with the current state of the art in conventional hyperspectral imaging (HSI),

with particular attention to methodologies, algorithms, and their limitations. On this basis,
we then examine spectral reconstruction, highlighting the advantages it provides as well
as the constraints that characterize it, with specific reference to the earliest applications
reported in the agri-food domain.
2. Literature Search and Study Selection Methodology
2.1. Databases, Publisher Platforms, and Coverage
We conducted structured searches on two citation databases—Web of Science Core
Collection and Scopus—and complemented them with Google Scholar to broaden recall, as
reported in Table 1. Full texts were retrieved on publisher platforms when available, with a
focus on ScienceDirect for Elsevier journals, and on MDPI, IEEE Xplore, SpringerLink,
and Wiley Online Library for non-Elsevier titles. These choices align with the venues
represented in our reference list (e.g., Elsevier journals such asInformation Fusion, Computers
and Electronics in Agriculture, and the Microchemical Journal).
2.2. Search Strategy and Keywords
Query strings combined controlled and free-text terms using Boolean operators and
truncation. Core terms were derived from the review scope and keywords of the manuscript
(“Spectral super-resolution”, “Multispectral Imaging”, “Hyperspectral Imaging”, “Deep
Learning”, “Precision Agriculture”, “Proximal sensing”, “On-field”) and were specialized
per context (HSI general, on-field HSI, SSR, algorithms/models). Queries were itera-
tively refined to balance precision (algorithm/dataset-specific terms) and recall (broader
agrifood terms).
2.3. Eligibility Criteria
Inclusion criteria: (i) peer-reviewed journal articles or full conference proceedings;
(ii) relevance to hyperspectral imaging in agrifood or to spectral super-resolution (RGB-to-
HSI/HSR) with agrifood applicability; (iii) English language; (iv) publication year 1998–
2025. Exclusion criteria: non-peer-reviewed items; purely satellite-only remote sensing
without proximal/on-field relevance; studies lacking spectral/agrifood focus; duplicates.

V ARIABLE PROJECTION METHOD

ABSTRACT
The problem of recovering a mixture of spike signals con-
volved with distinct kernels (point spread functions, PSFs)
lying on a parametric manifold, under the assumption that the
spike locations are known, is studied. We formulate the pro-
jected non-linear least squares estimator for kernel unmix-
ing and establish a lower bound on the radius of the region
of strong convexity in the presence of noise as a function of
the manifold coherence and Lipschitz properties, guarantee-
ing convergence and stability of the optimization program.
Numerical experiments highlight the role of the speed of de-
cay of the PSF class in the problem’s conditioning and con-
firm theoretical findings. Finally, we deploy the estimator
on real-world laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS)
data, removing the need for manual calibration and demon-
strating practical relevance.
Index Terms— non-convex optimization; PSF unmix-
ing; manifold constraint; variable projection method; laser-
induced breakdown spectroscopy
1. INTRODUCTION
Kernel or PSF unmixing is the problem of recovering a mix-
ture of spike signals after convolution with group-dependent
PSFs. Such parametric models arise in several areas of ap-
plied science and engineering, including super-resolution
imaging [1, 2], neural spike sorting [3, 4], multi-path chan-
nel identification in wireless communications [5, 6], and
calibration-free spectroscopy [7].
While blind deconvolution for a single modality has been
extensively studied [8], much less is known about sparse mix-
tures with multiple, unknown PSFs. Convex approaches [9,
10, 11] provide stable recovery guarantees but constrain the
PSFs to a predetermined low-dimensional subspace and are
computationally costly. Non-convex methods scale better [12,
13, 14], yet they typically rely on restrictive assumptions, of-
ten tied to Fourier-domain models. These limitations make
existing techniques ill-suited for applications such as laser-
induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS), where PSF shapes
reflect nonlinear plasma dynamics and do not conform to sim-
ple low-rank structures [15].
In [16], PSF unmixing with known spike support is tack-
led via nonlinear least squares. Coherence and interfer-
ence functions are introduced to control the loss geometry
and estimate the convergence regions of first-order opti-
mization methods. Our main contribution builds upon this
framework to introduce a novel projected nonlinear least
squares estimator based on the variable projection method
(VarPro) [17, 18, 19]. The separable structure of the model
is exploited through the use of the Moore–Penrose pseudo-
inverse, thereby obtaining a reduced and tractable problem
that is independent of the amplitude of the sources. We es-
tablish in Theorem 1 an explicit lower bound on the radius of
convergence around the ground truth in the presence of noise.
The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2,
the PSF unmixing problem is presented, and the separable
structure of the parameter is used to formulate a projected
non-linear least square estimator. Section 3.2 presents our
main result in Theorem 1, after introducing the notions of to-
tal coherence and Lipschitz continuity, which are needed to
control the optimisation landscape. A sketch proof is pro-
posed in Section 4. Finally, numerical experiments are con-
ducted in Section 5, confirming our theoretical findings. The
practical relevance of the approach in LIBS spectroscopy is
demonstrated, where it jointly estimates line widths and am-
plitudes, thereby removing the need for manual calibration
and automating a key step in quantitative analysis.

Theorem 1, we provided a lower bound on the size of the
strong basin of attraction in terms of problem parameters. We
